The Battle of White Rocks took place between 27 and 28 November 1944 in the locality of the same name, in the hamlet of Segno in the Italian municipality of Vado Ligure, in the province of Savona.
Background
The great roundup of 28 November 1944 was the most significant military event, if not the last of the great clashes that took place between partisans and Nazi-fascists, organised against the four Garibaldi Brigades : III - IV - V - VI, with the aim of annihilating the Savona partisan resistance. The Nazi-fascists believed, faced with the stasis of the situation on the war fronts by the Allied forces, that the final phase of the Second World War would be postponed to the spring of 1945, so, with the onset of winter they imagined they could destroy the partisan formations. Therefore on 25 November 1944, the Command of the 43rd German Division ordered the implementation of a large combing operation on the two sides of the Alpine ridge, that is on the Alpine maritime side to the west of Savona, on the heights of Vado Ligure, and on the more mountainous side in the western Alta Val Bormida, committing over 10,000 men to the operation. On the Alpine maritime side of Savona, units of the 5th San Marco Regiment were employed, supported by Black Brigades and GNR soldiers ; on the more mountainous side towards the upper Val Bormida, German soldiers were employed, supported by Black Brigades, GNR soldiers and Apennine Hunters.
The autumn-winter of 1944 was the period chosen by the Germans to launch massive and decisive actions against the partisan formations throughout the territory from Veneto to Lombardy, from Piedmont to Emilia, Liguria, Marche and Tuscany , knowing that the partisan movement was in a critical moment. The armed resistance, in fact, had been formed with the spontaneous but heterogeneous contribution of individuals and/or groups of people from different backgrounds (Italian army , political persecuted, political militants, young draft dodgers, fascist soldiers and San Marco deserters...), without a specific military training and with motivations that were not understood by everyone in the same way and longer times and greater availability of means would have been necessary to be able to better organize against an enemy that was well-organized militarily and equipped with automatic weapons. From the constitution of the "F. Calcagno" Detachment, which took place in November 1943 at Teccio del Tersè, to the formation of a Brigade, almost six months passed and it took almost a year before arriving at the constitution of the Division. Furthermore, starting from 13 November '44, the proclamation of General Alexander, Commander of the Allied Army in Italy, had had a negative impact, inviting the partisans to cease their activity to prepare for the new phase of the fight and to face the winter. The directives given were made public and repeated in various radio broadcasts: they produced dismay, resentment and heavy suspicions about the will of the Allies, especially Churchill, to reduce the partisan movement in Italy occupied by the Germans. These feelings particularly irritated the partisans linked to the parties, but also the workers who by now had joined the partisan cause. On the general organizational level of the partisan movement, a demobilization of people followed, which weakened some brigades and detachments: some went to increase the clandestine urban groups. This, however, did not compromise the overall stability of the organizational system, contrary to what the Nazi-fascists had hypothesized.
The partisan system had been reassured and supported by the success of the initiative called "the month of the partisan" that the entire population, together with the SAP of Vado Ligure and Quiliano, had organized. Despite the serious and dramatic economic situation in the country and entire families being destitute, 180,000 lire were collected to help the partisans in the mountains to survive and overcome the harsh winter, even if they were in unequal conditions compared to the enemy.
Battle
Despite information having been received from the SIM of the Corradini Brigade and from "trustworthy persons" of the gathering of soldiers for a roundup in the Savona - Vado Ligure - Altare area with troops from San Marco, German SS with police dogs, on the evening of 27 November 1944, a team from the Calcagno Detachment left the camp anyway to attack the barracks of the Guardia di Finanza , located in Porto Vado with the SAP teams from the "Ernesto Delitta", "Luigi Caroli" and "Santino Marcenaro" Detachments. The coup had been carefully planned by the Commander of the Calcagno Detachment, Tancredi Vallarino "Zazà", who had sent among others the volunteers Giovanni De Vita "Leo Carillo" ex officer of the San Marco, the volunteer Alfredo Masciari "Ventino" and the commander of the Clelia Corradini Brigade Dario Tonolini "Furio", who had availed himself of good elements of the SAP teams of Porto Vado, Valle and Sant'Ermete. The planned route, although it touched many areas under enemy control, had been monitored by the local SAP specialists. However, it was necessary to go past the Fornicoke factory, go up towards San Genesio , follow the path in the woods that led to Valgelata, go alongside the anti-aircraft battery and then go down towards the Aurelia. The route was carried out with precision and caution up to the barracks of the Guardia di Finanza next to the little church of Santa Maria della Visitazione. The loot recovered was huge: the guards were disarmed and two Breda machine guns were taken from the armoury , 26 revolvers which were then left to the SAP of the Corradini Brigade, 5 rifles, 40 muskets, a large quantity of ammunition and other field material. The return of the SAP members from the military action took place without problems: everything worked according to the foreseen plan. The meeting point was set in the Valley: from here the seized material was to leave again for Segno. The transport of all the war material was facilitated by the collection of a cart and a horse, which thanks to the interest of Claudio Pontacolone "Mirko" and Giulio Bertola "Busca" was not difficult to find. With the help of other sapists of the "Caroli" Detachment, Angelo, Giacomo, Giovanni, Nan and the commander Furio, all the material was moved to Segno. Here the sapists of the "Grillo" would then have thought of sending it to the "F. Calcagno" Detachment, which for about two months had camped in a wild hazelnut wood, overlooking the locality of Negrine. Once the transport was completed, the group of volunteers split up again to reach their respective detachments; the sapists of the "Caroli", who had followed the material up to Segno (Angelo, Giulio, Pietro, Giacomo, Giovanni, Nan, Claudio and Dario), climbed back into the empty cart and headed towards Sant'Ermete; The volunteers Leo Carillo and Ventino, after having paid their last respects to the partisan Vincenzo "Pippo" Pes, who was buried in the church of Segno, set off to go to the Calcagno Detachment. The return from the military operation was almost over when, having crossed the Sant'Ermete bridge, some soldiers appeared to them, almost at the first houses of "Né Ferré". Furio and Mirko managed to escape by jumping from the wagon and entering through a door on the road towards a vineyard; the others retraced their steps "up to the Pioa curve" and then took a path in the woods. Later, hidden by the trees, they recognized the San Marco soldiers in assault gear in two lines at the edge of the road; they therefore decided that it was better to go up to Segno along the path in the woods. In the sky, flares illuminated the heights towards Valleggia and towards the Sant'Ermete valley, testifying that the enemy search was underway. Angelo, Pietro, Giulio, with some volunteers from the "Grillo" decided to spend the night in a farmhouse in Segno.  The roundup generally involved the III, IV and VI Brigades with simultaneous attacks. The III Brigade engaged the enemy at Carpe, where the Torcello Detachment blocked the road by demolishing the "Salto del Lupo" bridge and blocking the progress of a convoy of armoured vehicles and cars ; the " Ines Negri " and "Torcello" Detachments, near Calizzano, engaged strong enemy contingents for two days inflicting heavy losses; the "Bonaguro" and "Bruzzone" Detachments, At the Melogno Pass and at Fort Settepani, they held the Germans, San Marco and Monterosa in check for another two days. The V Brigade lost its commander Bill, but was able to contain and fight from fixed positions. The VI Brigade, commanded by Antonio, unable to put up a valid resistance, after having moved with skilful maneuvers higher up in defense, escaped from the enemy. It was above all the IV Garibaldi Brigade commanded by "Enrico", Hermann Wygoda, comprising 3 Detachments, the "Maccari", the "Calcagno", and the "Rebagliati", for a total of 300 men, which succeeded with honor in not giving in to the shock of the great roundup.
Monument
The IV Brigade had fought strenuously, holding its positions, forcing the enemy to flee and leaving 300 men dead and wounded on the field. In the Garibaldina Brigade there were three dead: Giovanni De Vita "Leo Carillo", Carlo Cristoni "Diego" and Tornaghi Alfredo "Job"; there were two wounded: the Commander of the "Calcagno" Vallarino Tancredi "Zazà" and the Commander of the "Maccari" Armando Aiello "Piccolo"; there were also three prisoners among the volunteers: "Argo", "Irio", "Pino" and two among the SAP boys. The Municipalities of Vado Ligure and Quiliano, to remember the heroic battle at Rocche Bianche, suspended the mining activities of the stone quarry where the trench had been placed , contributed to valorising the site of the protruding rocks placed to defend the pass, which leads to the Tagliate, by obtaining a monumental hollow in stone. In 1946, thanks to the sculptor Achille Cabiati "Michelangelo", the Rocche Bianche were remembered with a white sculpture representing the "partisan breaking the chain". Subsequently, the names of the three fighters who fell during the roundup were carved on the Rock and then Calamandrei 's epigraph was placed on a plaque. In 1984, on the occasion of the 40th anniversary of the roundup at the Rocce Bianche, the partisan and artist Rivo Barsotti "Massa" created a copy of the sculpture The Partisan Breaking the Chain by A. Cabiati, but in reddish terracotta, with a plaque underneath containing the names of the three fallen in combat. After the act of vandalism committed in October 1994 by unknown naziskin against the symbols of partisan remembrance, the architect Carlo Daniele, on behalf of the ANPI, rebuilt the lower part of the monument (1995).
